en: **A Discourse on Resolving Doubts Regarding the Pure Land** Someone asked: "The teaching of the Pure Land is merely a symbolic representation of the Dharma; a person of wisdom should directly awaken to the Chan school."
"Now, you merely praise and speak of the Pure Land; will this not lead to attachment to phenomenal signs and a failure to clarify the rational nature? Answer:
"The nature of returning to the source is non-dual, yet the expedient means have many gates.
If you understand this principle, you will see that Chan and Pure Land are different paths leading to the same destination.
Your doubts will be resolved instantly, like ice melting."
In the past, people here have successively expounded upon this matter, not just once but many times.
As the Great Master Zhongfeng said:
"Chan is the Chan of Pure Land; [Pure Land is the Pure Land of Chan]."
"The Pure Land is the Pure Land of Chan;
those who cultivate it must value entering deeply through a single gate.
These few words are an even more enduring and immutable thesis for ten thousand generations.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, having attained the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha, said:
"By means of the mind that mindfulness of the Buddha, one enters the patience of non-arising.
And the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, having entered the inconceivable liberation of the Avataṃsaka, said:
"May I, at the end of my life, be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.

These two great beings—one attending the Teacher of the Sahā world and the other attending the Guide of the Land of Peaceful Nurturing—should each establish their own distinct approaches; yet they are harmonized and interfused, with neither obstructing the other. This is something commonly heard and well known to all people; how can one still cling to partial views?
Furthermore, you say:
"The Pure Land symbolizes the Dharma. Is it not the case that the pure mind itself is the Pure Land; how could there be yet another world of seven treasures?
Then one would say that a virtuous mind is itself heaven—how could there be any further Yāma or Trāyastriṃśa heavens?
And that an evil mind is itself hell—how could there be any further swords, blades, cauldrons, or boiling water?
A mind of ignorance is itself an animal; how could there be anything further such as possessing hair or horns?
"Furthermore, you delight in discussing the principle of nature (li-xing) while wearying of speaking about phenomenal characteristics (shi-xiang)."
It is all because you wish to manifest that you belong to a high tradition, fearing that others might say you do not penetrate the principle of nature (li-xing). Alas!

If you were truly one whose understanding of the principle of nature is clear and penetrating, you would know that there is no principle apart from phenomena and no nature apart from appearances; they have been fundamentally interpenetrating from the beginning. Why must you insist on abandoning phenomena to seek the principle, or leaving appearances to find the nature?
Moreover, the Buddha-lands are divided into four types; do you truly believe that there is only the Land of Quiescent Light (Sambhogakāya) and no lands of True Reward or Adornment?

If one considers it lofty merely to speak exclusively of the discourse on formlessness, then those of even slightly sharp faculties could achieve this by simply reading two versions of the sutras and treatises and memorizing a few koans—what difficulty would that pose?
Moreover, since you have already thoroughly realized your own mind, every place is a pure land.
Let me test you with this question:
"Would you be willing to dwell and reside right within a latrine?"
Would you be willing to share a trough with dogs, pigs, horses, and oxen for food and drink?
Would you be willing to enter burial mounds and sleep among the stinking, decaying corpses?
"Are you willing to wash and nurse those afflicted with kāmalā disease, or those suffering from foul ailments such as pus, blood, excrement, and urine, for many months and years?
Regarding these matters, he remained joyful and at ease, paying them little heed, and granted your request to speak of the high mountains and level plains throughout the Western Regions.

If one outwardly pretends to practice forbearance while inwardly harboring doubt and resentment, it means that the distinction between the pure and the defiled has not yet been emptied and feelings of hatred and attachment still persist; yet, to then open one's mouth to loftily discourse upon the transcendent realm of the Great Sage, while denying the existence of Buddha-lands and disparaging rebirth therein—this may be called deceiving Heaven and deluding others, choosing to remain willfully ignorant of oneself.

Alas! Alas! Furthermore, if you possess great power and have made a great vow, wishing to emerge and submerge yourself again and again within the ocean of birth and death while practicing the bodhisattva path without fear or cowardice, then my rebirth in the Pure Land shall not be forced upon you.
Perhaps you fear that the winds of sensory objects in this land are so vast that you cannot act as their master;
or that the appearance of Buddhas in the world is so difficult to encounter that there will be no means for you to practice and study;
or that your power of patience is not yet firm, such that you cannot liberate sentient beings from the perilous places within the triple world.
I reflect that although this retribution-body may exhaust its span, it cannot forever sever birth and death so as not to undergo future existence;
yet since future existence still persists, when one discards this body and receives the next, the path ahead is vast and desolate, and I do not know where I shall go.
To abandon this Pure Land and fail to be reborn there is no small error.

"This Dharma-gate of the Pure Land appears shallow yet is profound; it appears near yet is distant; it appears difficult yet is easy; it appears easy yet is difficult. You shall know this for yourself in the future."
Whether you now practice Chan meditation or recite the Buddha’s name, it is perfectly fine to enter deeply through whichever gate suits you.

However, you must avoid mistaking brass for gold or being content with a mere trifle; such attitudes resemble the narrow understanding of one peering through a tube, leading to reckless and arbitrary talk that ends up disparaging the Pure Land.

It is like a foolish and mad son who reviles and insults his parents; though his parents, out of compassionate pity, do not reprimand him, how can he escape the fact that natural law does not tolerate such acts and the royal law must execute him?
The retribution for such false speakers is likewise.
How truly fearsome! How truly lamentable!

Postscript to the *Discernment of Doubts Regarding the Pure Land*: The layman Wei Xiu resounded the Way of Learning in Jingjiang, where the refined air of music and instruction from Wucheng prevailed.
Having retired from official service, he exerted his refined energy to carve the Sanskrit manuscripts into printed volumes for the convenience of study;
furthermore, he widely propagated and praised the Pure Land teachings by carving the *Yibian* (Discourse on Doubts) that I had authored, ensuring its broad circulation.

Now, to hold fast to the aspiration within the gates of the ten mysteries and to cause the spirit to dwell in the realm of the nine lotuses—this may be called being profoundly in accord with the King of Vows of Samantabhadra and wondrously entering the ocean of the nature of Vairocana.
It is a pity that he passed away prematurely, not allowing Cao Luchuan to see him.
